papers.title: How Language Models Learn Taste: Brand Preference in LLMs
papers.abstract: Asked to name a running shoe brand, language models say Nike. Asked to recommend one, they say Brooks. This paper asks where models learn that taste. Across 102 models and 42 brand categories, the brand a model picks when recommending differs from the brand it names in 26. The field moves together to a shared recommendation. The Named brands are market leaders, and the Picked brands are mostly niche and specialist. Three open training pipelines show where this forms. Pretraining already attaches the recommended brand to advice. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to answer and mostly leaves the pick unchanged. Preference optimization (DPO) teaches the model which answer is better, and the pick moves in all three pipelines, by 11 to 24 points. The preference data contains almost no brands. DPO moves the model's judgments toward a second set of associations even when the preferred brand is not in the preference data, and the effect reaches beyond brands. Asked to choose a sauce, models switch from ketchup to pesto. We do not know exactly how these preferences arise. We suspect they come from the judge models that decide which answers count as better during preference training. For brands, a recommendation depends less on what a model knows about them than on whether they fit this taste.
papers.summary: Ask a model to name a running-shoe brand and it says Nike; ask it to recommend one and it says Brooks. Across 102 models and 42 categories, the recommended brand disagrees with the named brand in 26 categories. Named brands are mostly market leaders; picked brands are mostly niche specialists. Across three open training pipelines, pretraining already attaches the recommended brand to advice-style prompts, SFT mostly leaves the pick unchanged, and DPO moves it by 11–24 points in every pipeline. The preference data contains almost no brand comparisons, yet DPO still shifts judgments—even sauce choices from ketchup to pesto. ==Recommendation taste forms mainly in preference optimization, not only from what the model “knows” about brands==.

deep_reading.title: How Language Models Learn Taste: Brand Preference in LLMs
deep_reading.content:
Ask a language model to "name a running shoe brand" and it says Nike; ask it to "recommend one" and it says Brooks. The author tested 102 models across 42 brand categories. Under a two-turn "recommend, then pick one" question, the panel's brand differs from the "name one" brand in 26 categories, and **models from different labs move together to the same brand**: Delta becomes Singapore Airlines, Chrome becomes Firefox, Google becomes DuckDuckGo. The Named brands are mostly market leaders; the Picked ones are mostly niche or specialist. Using three open pipelines that release a checkpoint after every training stage, the paper traces where this "taste" forms: pretraining already ties the recommended brand to advice contexts, SFT mostly leaves the pick unchanged, and ==DPO moves the pick by 11 to 24 points in all three pipelines==, even though DPO's preference data contains almost no brands. The shift is not limited to brands: when OLMo 3 7B is asked to "choose a sauce", the share choosing pesto rises from 5% at base to 67% after DPO.

![The paper's Table 1: from naming to picking (102 models, 42 categories). "Consensus moved" counts categories where the panel's most common answer differs from its answer under Name; "Answer unchanged" is the share of a model's answers matching its own most common answer under Name.](figs/2610.28272/crop_tab1.png)

## 1. The problem: where do a model's recommendations come from?

More and more people simply ask an AI assistant to "recommend a such-and-such". Existing audits examine which brands production assistants surface and how stable those answers are across rewordings, but few ask at which training stage those preferences form. This paper starts from a simple contrast: "name one" asks what comes to mind first, while "recommend one" asks for a judgment. When the answers differ, the model is using a different set of associations to judge.

## 2. Experimental design

**Questions.** There are 42 categories, from soda to cloud providers. Each is asked with three verbs, all requiring a single name: Name ("Name a running shoe brand"), Choose ("Choose one") and Recommend ("Can you recommend one?"). A two-turn question first asks "Can you recommend a running shoe brand?" and then "Which one would you pick?". The four answers are called the Named, Chosen, Recommended and Picked brands.

**Panel.** 102 models are queried through OpenRouter at temperature 1; one-name questions run 8 times per model and category, the two-turn question 4 times, and 25 hybrid reasoning models are also run with reasoning off. Data was collected from 2026-09-30 to 2026-10-10. Perplexity Sonar, which answers from live search, is excluded.

**Scoring.** A one-name reply must be a single name, with no list or lead-in. A two-turn reply is reduced to the brand it commits to; a list, a question back or a refusal counts as no pick, which happens in 17% of two-turn replies. On three hand-checked samples, the rules agreed with a human reading on 87% to 97% of replies.

## 3. Finding one: the panel names one brand and picks another

Each step toward judgment changes the panel's brand in more categories: 6/42 for Choose, 16/42 for Recommend and 26/42 for the two-turn pick. Meanwhile, a model's own Named brand falls from 89% of its answers to 31% of its picks. Each question has its own consensus: under Name the most common brand takes 76% of answers, and between 60% and 69% for the others.

![The paper's Table 2: the panel's brand under each question in the 26 categories where the Picked brand differs from the Named brand.](figs/2610.28272/crop_tab2.png)

The Named brands are market leaders such as Google, Walmart, McDonald's, Facebook and Verizon. The Picked brands are mostly smaller ones with a specialist or insider following, such as DuckDuckGo, Aldi, Sierra Nevada, Reddit, Signal and Brooks, plus a few premium brands, such as Hermès over Chanel and Hyatt over Marriott.

Models do not reject their default; they demote it. In the two-turn pick, a model's own Named brand appears in its recommendation list 83% of the time but is picked only 31% of the time; when listed, it comes first in 60% of lists and is picked in 37%. With a median list of 4 brands, a random draw would pick it 30% of the time. In each of the 12 labs with at least three models, the two-turn pick changes the lab's consensus brand in 55% to 74% of categories, so every major lab shares the pattern.

Two side observations. Labs favour their own AI assistant: asked to recommend one, Anthropic's models answer Claude 92% of the time, other labs' models 15%. But labs do not favour their other products; Google's models recommend Google search and Chrome less often than other labs' models do. And in a spot check, Claude Opus 5.5 answered the two-turn question for all 42 categories with web search available, searched in none, and left the Named brand in 25 of the 26 categories where the panel does.

## 4. Finding two: taste forms when a model learns which answer is better

OLMo 3 7B, OLMo 3.1 32B and Tulu 3 8B release checkpoints for every stage: base, SFT, DPO and RL. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning releases only a base and a final model. Scoring uses log-probabilities, so every stage and category can be measured without sampling.

**Pretraining supplies the candidates.** A base model cannot be asked for advice, but it can complete an advice sentence. Given "If you want a good web browser, I recommend", Tulu's base model continues with Firefox in 13 of 20 samples; given "A well-known web browser is", it continues with Chrome in 10. Over the 16 categories where the Recommended brand differs from the Named one, advice phrasing raises the Recommended brand's share in 7 to 10 categories, depending on the base model, and lowers it in at most one.

**SFT leaves the pick; DPO moves it.** To compare the same choice across stages, every stage gets the same three-item list (Named brand, Picked brand and a third recommended brand) with "Which one would you pick?", the reply starts with "I'd pick", and the probability of each brand is read off. Each list is shown in both orders because base models favour the first-listed brand.

| Pipeline | Base | SFT | DPO | RL | SFT→DPO (90% interval) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| OLMo 3 7B | 58% | 52% | 76% | 74% | +24 [+16, +33] |
| Tulu 3 8B | 54% | 58% | 69% | 68% | +11 [+6, +16] |
| OLMo 3.1 32B | 63% | 57% | 73% | 73% | +16 [+7, +25] |

The figures are the probability of picking the Picked brand over the Named brand across the 26 categories. After SFT all sit near base; the DPO step raises all three significantly, and RL keeps what DPO set. Nemotron rises from 58% at base to 79% in its final model.

The move does not depend on which brands the panel picks. Across all 42 categories, a brand's base-model log-probability under Name correlates negatively with how much DPO raises it under Recommend (-0.16, -0.14 and -0.23 across the three pipelines, each interval below zero): **DPO lifts the brands the base model found less obvious**. Yet DPO does not lower obvious answers everywhere: in the 16 categories where the panel keeps the Named brand, its share does not fall at DPO in any pipeline. Repeating the test on the SFT stage's own recommendation lists, the DPO step remains at +14, +9 and +14 points.

## 5. Finding three: the preference data holds almost no brands

OLMo 3's and Tulu 3's training data are public. The author searched for requests that pair one of the 26 categories with an advice word such as "recommend", "best" or "which". In 260,000 OLMo 3 DPO pairs, the chosen answer names the Picked brand 3 times and the rejected answer once; Tulu 3 is just as sparse. DPO did not learn these picks from brand examples, though indirect associations elsewhere in the data cannot be ruled out.

The same move appears outside brands. Using Name and Choose questions on everyday categories (a tree, a smell, an animal and so on), the author measures the same log-probability shift on the 23 categories where the panel's answers differ. Base models barely separate the two verbs, and DPO pushes Choose toward the panel's answer in all three pipelines, with SFT→DPO increments of +0.39, +0.11 and +0.17 nats. When OLMo 3 7B chooses a sauce, pesto goes from 5% at base to 27% after SFT and 67% after DPO, while ketchup falls from 72% to 6%.

**Who defines "better"?** Half of OLMo 3's DPO pairs are judged by an LLM; the other half pair a Qwen 3 32B response as chosen with one from a much smaller model as rejected. Tulu 3's pairs are rated by GPT-4o. The author therefore suspects the taste comes from the judge models used in preference training. Tulu 3 has a single judge, which allows a test: in categories where GPT-4o recommends a different brand from Tulu's base-model favourite, DPO moves the pick toward GPT-4o's brand by 8 points (90% interval 2 to 14). Note that the GPT-4o queried is the current release, not the 2024-08-06 snapshot that labelled Tulu's data, so this is an approximation.

## 6. Limitations and what it means in practice

The paper lists its limitations: the questions are short and carry no personal context, and measures on short prompts may not predict real use; the three staged pipelines come from one lab and share much of their recipe, so the formation path is shown only on them, though the 102-model panel shows the phenomenon itself extends beyond them; Nemotron has no intermediate stages; the 32B model and Nemotron ran at 8-bit precision; for OLMo 3 7B, sampled picks place the change at RL rather than DPO; and the panel is a snapshot of late September to early October 2026. In addition, "judge models transmit taste" is the author's conjecture, and the 8-point Tulu result is partial evidence. The AI-usage note states that Claude (Opus 5.5) was used to run probes, build the analysis and draft the text, while several Claude models are also study subjects.

There are direct implications for two groups. **For post-training teams**: preference optimization changes a model's judgments in domains its preference data never covers, likely via the judge models. If your product involves recommendation or choice (shopping assistants, local services, travel planning), run a "name vs. recommend" probe set at every training stage, monitor the shift around DPO, and examine the judge model's own preferences. **For brands and marketers**: the author concludes that whether a brand gets recommended ==depends less on what a model knows about it than on whether it fits the model's implicit taste==. In marketing terms this is a matter of brand associations and positioning, but how a brand can build such associations for itself is left to future work.

papers.title: A Cue's Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers
papers.authors: Felix Buecheler, Gerardo Berbeglia, Mingyu Guo
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly asked to shop on a user's behalf, which lets seller-controlled content such as badges, endorsements, and framing steer what they recommend. That poses the question at the core of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller content shifts an agent's choice, but how much. The usual gauge of that influence, how often a cue wins the choice, has a blind spot: once a cue is strong enough to be picked almost every time, the choice rate can no longer show how much stronger one cue is than another. We introduce price-equivalent (PE) auditing, which removes this ceiling by pricing the cue in money. In a counterbalanced, position-controlled forced choice, we raise the cued product's price until it is chosen only half the time, and report that premium as the cue's price-equivalent: a formally defined, policy-conditioned parity threshold that makes very different cues comparable. Priced this way, cues that look equally strong at equal price differ by a wide margin, so choice-rate audits substantially under-resolve seller influence. We run the audit over 113,472 trials, seven models across families, and two product categories. To our knowledge, we also run the first price-equivalent audit of a decision-native model, Jev, which outputs a choice probability directly instead of generating text; strikingly, its profile is unlike any text model we tested, resisting most cues yet remaining susceptible to the strongest social-proof claims. We release the stimuli, logs, and code as a benchmark that reports each model's cue-price profile rather than a single score, giving developers and auditors a common, reproducible way to measure how content moves AI shopping agents.
papers.summary: When an LLM shops for a user, seller cues such as “best-seller,” endorsements, or scarcity can steer its pick. Choice-rate audits hit a ceiling once a cue already wins near 100% of the time. Price-equivalent (PE) auditing raises the cued product’s price in a counterbalanced forced choice until it is chosen only half the time, and reports that premium as the cue’s PE. Across 113,472 trials, seven models, and two categories, cues that look equally strong by choice rate can differ several-fold in PE. The decision-native model Jev resists most cues yet still bends to the strongest social-proof claims. ==Pricing seller content in money makes different cues comparable==.

deep_reading.title: A Cue's Hidden Price: Auditing Seller Influence on AI Shoppers
deep_reading.content:
At equal price, GPT-4o chose the headphones carrying "Our best-selling model, chosen by over 10,000 customers" in all 144 trials. Its price had to rise by about 13% (roughly $17 on a $130 item) before its selection share fell to one half. A plain neutral sentence was also chosen almost 100% of the time at equal price, but it was abandoned at a premium of about 2%. The University of Adelaide authors argue that **the usual choice-rate audit has a ceiling**: strong cues all sit near 100% and cannot be told apart. The paper proposes price-equivalent (PE) auditing, which prices a seller cue in money: raise the cued product's price until it is chosen only half the time, and that premium is the cue's PE. Across 7 models, 2 categories and 113,472 trials, ==six conditions all chosen at ≥95% at equal price span PEs from 1.6% to 21.4%==, and the choice-rate ranking can even flip.

![Both cues win ~100% at equal price; the sweep separates them: the neutral sentence crosses 0.5 near 2%, strong social proof near 13%.](figs/2610.25843/hf2.png)

## 1. The problem: how much more will content make a shopping agent pay

LLMs are moving from answering questions to acting for users, browsing, comparing and buying. Once the decision-maker is a model, the seller's lever shifts from persuading a person to steering an agent. A "best-seller" badge, an expert endorsement, or a different phrasing of a spec can all tilt the agent toward a product. The authors treat such a cue as a **hidden discount**: like a price cut it raises the product's chance of being chosen, but the price is unchanged and the buyer cannot see it. This is the core question of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller content moves agents, but by how much.

Prior work mostly reports influence as a change in choice probability, a scale that misleads where it matters. Strong cues push the choice rate to nearly 100% and become indistinguishable; after position balancing, primacy is averaged into 50%, which looks like indifference. Knowing a cue "raised the choice rate" does not tell you whether it is worth pennies or a large share of the price.

## 2. Method: price-equivalent auditing

**Task.** A product pair is matched on price, star rating, rating count and specs; only one carries an appended cue sentence. In a two-alternative choice the authors record the equal-price probability of choosing the cued product, then raise its price in 8 steps: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 18, 26%, denser near zero where most crossings fall. The PE is the premium, as a percentage of the base price, at which the cued product's selection share falls to one half.

**Formal definition.** Given a model and prompt environment $M$ and a pair distribution $Q$, the auditor fixes a presentation policy $\pi$ that sets which product carries the cue and whether it is listed first or second; the paper uses a balanced policy with each of the four states at 1/4. With $S_Q(g)$ the cued product's selection probability at premium $g$ averaged over $\pi$,

$${\rm PE}_Q(c_1{:}c_0\mid M,\pi)=\inf\{g:S_Q(g)\le\tfrac12\}$$

The authors stress that PE depends on the cue contrast, products, presentation policy, model, prompt and decoding configuration, and in general cannot be read as an individual indifference point or willingness to pay.

**Estimation and censoring.** The primary estimator is model-free: linear interpolation between the two neighbouring price points where the pooled curve crosses 0.5. Because the equal-price choice is often 1, a global logistic fit would be distorted. A cue already dispreferred at equal price (choice rate below 0.5) is reported as PE ≤ 0; a curve that never falls to one half within 26% is right-censored to a lower bound. Confidence intervals use a bootstrap resampled by product pair; with only 6 pairs, intervals may be too narrow.

**Position control.** In every (pair, price-point) cell the cued product is first in half the trials and second in the other half, and the cue sits on A and B equally often, with 6 calls in each of the four states.

**Setup.** A cue is one sentence appended to a neutral description. The set covers four intensities of social proof ("A popular choice." up to "The #1 best-selling model, chosen by over 100,000 customers."), scarcity ("Only a few left in stock."), authority ("Recommended by audio experts."), information-preserving rephrasings (percent vs fraction, a rescaled rating, and gain/loss framing "9 out of 10 buyers keep it." vs "1 out of 10 buyers returns it."), plus neutral, vacuous, length-matched and presence controls. Products are 6 headphone pairs ($59.99–$199.99) and 6 coffee-machine pairs ($49.99–$299.99). Models are strong/weak pairs from four providers: GPT-4o/GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet/Haiku, Nova Pro/Micro, Llama-3.3-70B/3.1-8B. Nova Pro is excluded for a high non-response rate (21%), and Llama-3.1-8B, which picks the first option in about 97% of trials, is excluded from cross-model claims. Temperature is 0.7 with 24 repetitions per (pair, price point), so one condition is $6\times8\times24=1152$ trials.

## 3. Core finding: price separates what choice rates cannot

On GPT-4o, each cue condition is plotted on two axes: the equal-price choice rate a conventional audit would report, and the PE.

![Equal-price choice rate vs price-equivalent per cue condition (GPT-4o, headphones): six conditions sit at ≥0.95 yet span 1.6–21.4% PE; gain/loss framing has the highest PE but a lower choice rate than the saturated cues.](figs/2610.25843/hf3.png)

The sharpest case is **scarcity**. At equal price its choice rate is 0.95, higher than gain/loss framing's 0.72, yet its PE is only 1.6% against 22.3% for gain/loss, a fourteenfold gap with disjoint intervals. A choice-rate audit ranks the two the wrong way round. The authors note this is not a precision problem that more trials would fix: the two quantities measure different things, how often a cue wins when price is tied and how much price it can absorb. A cue can be "broad and shallow" (scarcity) or "narrow and deep" (gain/loss framing), and only the latter is what a seller can convert into money.

**GPT-4o cue price list (PE, %):**

| Cue | Headphones | Coffee |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Social proof: weak | 0.7 | 1.1 |
| Social proof: moderate | 1.3 | 1.8 |
| Social proof: strong | 12.9 | 15.0 |
| Social proof: very strong | 21.4 | 21.4 |
| Authority (domain-matched) | 19.8 | 21.6 |
| Scarcity | 1.6 | 1.5 |
| Gain/loss framing | 22.3 | 26+ |

| Presence control | 0.9 | 0.6 |

A few readings. The four social-proof intensities give a monotone, sharply nonlinear PE: weak and moderate sit near zero and the premium switches on only at "strong", and on headphones the three lower tiers have non-overlapping intervals, evidence that the instrument tracks persuasive strength. The length-matched control at about 10.6% shows the premium comes from the sentence's meaning, not from an extra sentence. The model is indifferent to number-preserving rewrites (rating rescale, percent to fraction) yet strongly swayed by a gain/loss framing of the same fact: **it responds to the form of a statement, not to its information**. The whole pattern replicates on coffee machines; authority reaches about 21.6% when domain-matched, but "recommended by audio experts" on a coffee machine is only about 1.9%, so the model cares whether authority is relevant. A length-matched $2^3$ factorial over social proof, authority and scarcity detects no interaction, consistent with additivity, though with only 6 pairs moderate interactions cannot be ruled out.

## 4. Across models, position bias and a native decision model

**Across models.** On the six task-engaged models social proof keeps its step pattern: the weak and moderate tiers stay at or below 4%, and at least one strong tier lies clearly above; scarcity commands at most 2% on any model. Yet at equal price GPT-4o and GPT-4o mini prefer the scarcity product (0.95, 0.88) while Claude Sonnet finds it aversive (0.19). Raw authority (1.6–19.8%) and gain/loss (0–22.3%) PEs look wildly different, but PE combines cue pull with price sensitivity: at +10%, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet and Llama-3.3-70B almost never keep the pricier identical product, while Nova Micro does about half the time. Claude Sonnet's 1.6% authority PE reflects a steep price response, not an unmoved model; Nova Micro keeps choosing the cued product at more than double the price, so its PE is unidentified and its apparent susceptibility is price-insensitivity. Raw PE should not be ranked across models.

**Position bias.** GPT-4o picks the first option in 56.3% of all trials, rising to about 65% in low-signal conditions. After balancing, the pooled PE is the crossing of the averaged curves, not the mean of the two slot crossings: scarcity is 6.1% when first, 0.9% when second, and 1.6% pooled. The authors also price "first slot" itself: at most 3.2% on price-sensitive models, 14.0% on GPT-4o mini, and beyond 80% on the price-blind Nova Micro and Llama-3.1-8B. This is a warning to any practice that reads preferences off LLM choices, including LLM-as-judge.

**How much wording matters.** Twelve truthful, LLM-generated rewrites of one full description (all weaving in strong social proof and scarcity) move GPT-4o's PE between 2.3% and 8.0%. Wording is a real lever, but several times smaller than the choice of cue (0.7–21.4%). Under four equivalent task phrasings the social-proof ordering holds, but strong-cue premia drift by up to about 8 points. Selecting the top-PE cue among 9 on 5 headphone pairs, its out-of-sample PE is 13.3 points above the mean of the nine.

**Native decision model Jev.** Jev returns a probability per option rather than generating text. The ceiling replicates: four cues are chosen in every equal-price trial yet span 1.5–16.6% once priced (headphones). Its profile differs from every text model: social proof switches on only at "very strong" (15.4%), authority is worth 1.5% (19.8% for GPT-4o), and gain/loss framing is worth 0; the off-domain "audio experts" sentence on a coffee machine is never chosen at equal price in 144 trials. Input format also changes Jev's prices: passing cards as a structured object raised strong social proof from 2.0% to 10.8%.

## 5. Five rules for auditing in practice

The authors distil their results into reusable operating rules: counterbalance position and cue target within every cell; read the equal-price rate as a two-sided validity gate, where every cue near 0.5 signals a model not engaging the task and exactly 1.00 signals an axis with no resolution left; always run a cue-free price-only control, since PE is the ratio of cue pull to price sensitivity; mark censoring explicitly, because a censored value is a bound and must not enter a ranking; and read PE as ordinal-to-interval, where rankings and coarse bands are trustworthy but exact percentages are not.

## 6. Limitations and industry relevance

The paper states its limits plainly. It is a controlled synthetic two-alternative choice that measures susceptibility under clean conditions and does not predict a live shopping environment, where cues compete with search, reviews and multi-step navigation. "Non-human" is a contrast with the persuasion literature, not a matched human baseline. Scarcity was tested in one formulation, so its low PE means low for that sentence, not immunity. Each condition has only 6 product pairs, both categories are consumer-electronics durables, and services such as travel or lodging are untested. The models are a convenience sample, so claims hold for these models only. The authors also acknowledge the tool is dual-use: it serves governance and auditing as well as agent-facing content optimization. Their line is truthfulness, with every cue a sentence plausibly true of the product, and they release logs, stimuli and code but not a turnkey library of optimized manipulative descriptions.

For teams building shopping agents or running e-commerce platforms, three takeaways stand out. First, when checking whether an agent is being steered, do not look only at choice rates; add a price axis, or strong cues all pile up at the ceiling. Second, ==position bias is itself a platform-owned, priceable channel==, and ranking policies deserve the same audit as cues. Third, do not carry an audit from one model to another; measure its price sensitivity first. The code and data are open, so the protocol can be re-run directly on your own models and categories.

A plain neutral sentence was also chosen almost 100% of the time at equal price, but it was abandoned at a premium of about 2%. The University of Adelaide authors argue that the usual choice-rate audit has a ceiling: strong cues all sit near 100% and cannot be told apart. The paper proposes price-equivalent (PE) auditing, which prices a seller cue in money: raise the cued product's price until it is chosen only half the time, and that premium is the cue's PE. Across 7 models, 2 categories and 113,472 trials, six conditions all chosen at ≥95% at equal price span PEs from 1.6% to 21.4%, and the choice-rate ranking can even flip.

1. The problem: how much more will content make a shopping agent pay

LLMs are moving from answering questions to acting for users, browsing, comparing and buying. Once the decision-maker is a model, the seller's lever shifts from persuading a person to steering an agent. A "best-seller" badge, an expert endorsement, or a different phrasing of a spec can all tilt the agent toward a product. The authors treat such a cue as a hidden discount: like a price cut it raises the product's chance of being chosen, but the price is unchanged and the buyer cannot see it. This is the core question of generative engine optimization (GEO): not whether seller content moves agents, but by how much.

Prior work mostly reports influence as a change in choice probability, a scale that misleads where it matters. Strong cues push the choice rate to nearly 100% and become indistinguishable; after position balancing, primacy is averaged into 50%, which looks like indifference. Knowing a cue "raised the choice rate" does not tell you whether it is worth pennies or a large share of the price.

2. Method: price-equivalent auditing

Task. A product pair is matched on price, star rating, rating count and specs; only one carries an appended cue sentence. In a two-alternative choice the authors record the equal-price probability of choosing the cued product, then raise its price in 8 steps: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 18, 26%, denser near zero where most crossings fall. The PE is the premium, as a percentage of the base price, at which the cued product's selection share falls to one half.

Formal definition. Given a model and prompt environment M and a pair distribution Q, the auditor fixes a presentation policy π that sets which product carries the cue and whether it is listed first or second; the paper uses a balanced policy with each of the four states at 1/4. With SQ​(g) the cued product's selection probability at premium g averaged over π,
PEQ​(c1​:c0​∣M,π)=inf{g:SQ​(g)≤21​}
The authors stress that PE depends on the cue contrast, products, presentation policy, model, prompt and decoding configuration, and in general cannot be read as an individual indifference point or willingness to pay.

Estimation and censoring. The primary estimator is model-free: linear interpolation between the two neighbouring price points where the pooled curve crosses 0.5. Because the equal-price choice is often 1, a global logistic fit would be distorted. A cue already dispreferred at equal price (choice rate below 0.5) is reported as PE ≤ 0; a curve that never falls to one half within 26% is right-censored to a lower bound. Confidence intervals use a bootstrap resampled by product pair; with only 6 pairs, intervals may be too narrow.

Position control. In every (pair, price-point) cell the cued product is first in half the trials and second in the other half, and the cue sits on A and B equally often, with 6 calls in each of the four states.

Products are 6 headphone pairs ($59.99–$199.99) and 6 coffee-machine pairs ($49.99–$299.99). Nova Pro is excluded for a high non-response rate (21%), and Llama-3.1-8B, which picks the first option in about 97% of trials, is excluded from cross-model claims. Temperature is 0.7 with 24 repetitions per (pair, price point), so one condition is 6×8×24=1152 trials.

papers.title: LLM Multi-Agent Systems Are Vulnerable to Herding and Runaway Cascades
papers.authors: Farnoosh Hashemi, Shiyu Ji, Joice Chen, Michael W. Macy
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-agent systems where they collaborate by responding to others' choices, creating endogenous feedback loops with vulnerability to social influence, herding behavior and runaway cascades. Following the design of the classic Music Lab experiment, we tested this vulnerability in large populations of LLM agents that recommended unfamiliar songs, with or without exposure to cumulative recommendation counts. Exposure led to runaway cascades that generated extreme and unpredictable collective recommendations increasingly divergent from a song's intrinsic appeal. Compared to humans, LLM populations were generally far more susceptible to herding behavior, and unlike humans, LLM cascades were less able to self-correct. This vulnerability has implications for multi-agent collaboration in recommender systems, automated evaluation, complex problem-solving, and unauthorized conspiracies.
papers.summary: When LLM agents recommend unfamiliar songs and can see cumulative recommendation counts, they form herding cascades like the classic Music Lab. Seeing counts makes collective picks diverge from a song’s intrinsic appeal into extreme, unpredictable outcomes. LLM populations herd more readily than humans and correct themselves less. ==Visible popularity among agents amplifies feedback loops instead of converging on intrinsic quality==.

papers.title: Prompting Strategy Effects Depend on the Judge: A Multilingual Study of LLM-as-a-Judge Robustness
papers.authors: Asal Mehrabi, Mohammad Aliannejadi, Clemencia Siro
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation is increasingly applied to multilingual tasks, yet prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought and Role Conditioning are recommended based solely on English benchmarks. Whether their effectiveness transfers across judge models and languages remains unknown: prompt-sensitivity studies are largely English-centric, while existing multilingual judge studies fix the prompt template. In this work, we address this gap by measuring this interaction through a benchmark of 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets, yielding over 1M pointwise scores on gold-reference outputs, validated against human judgments. We find that prompting strategies are not transferable: the choice of the judge model dominates the choice of prompting strategy, strategy effects reverse direction across judges, and stability degrades in low-resource languages, where these effects are concealed by aggregate reporting. These findings show that prompting effects in multilingual evaluation are conditioned on the judge, task, and language. Consequently, prompting strategies should be validated for the intended evaluation setting, and cross-study comparisons should account for both judge and prompt configuration.
papers.summary: Multilingual LLM-as-a-Judge setups often reuse prompting tricks validated only in English. This study runs 9 prompting strategies, 4 open-weight judges, 27 languages, and 4 tasks across 13 datasets for >1M pointwise scores against gold references, checked with human judgments. Prompting strategies do not transfer: the judge model dominates the prompt choice, the same strategy can reverse across judges, and stability drops in low-resource languages. ==Validate prompts for the intended judge, task, and language instead of copying English defaults==.
